newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada jobs, productivity growth seen for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Canada jobs, productivity growth seen for 1997.

text.p: Canada should see strong growth in productivity and jobs over the next year, the chief economist of Royal Bank of Canada said on Friday.
"We are reasonably optimistic about the Canadian economy over the next little while," John McCallum told economists at a forum in Ottawa.
He said Canada's gross domestic product should grow by about three percent in 1997. He predicted the creation of about 700,000 jobs over the next two years.

Much of Canada's recent economic expansion stemmed from strong exports, but exports would not be as strong in 1997 because of weaker demand by the United States, Canada's largest trading partner, McCallum said.
The growth "has to be from some combination of consumption and investment," he said.
Consumer confidence should pick up gradually as Canadians react to lower interest rates, McCallum said.
"The consumer has been quite traumatized" and needed to recover for Canada's economy to be healthy, he said.
He said he doubted the Bank of Canada would follow the U.S. Federal Reserve if it raised interest rates next week.

"My guess is the Bank of Canada will not follow," McCallum said. "We don't think the Bank of Canada will tighten at all before the end of 1997. We think the low rate environment will be here for some time."
He predicted the Canadian dollar would strengthen modestly to about US$0.75 by the end of 1997 and to about US$0.78 or US$0.79 by next year.
He said unemployment rates were difficult to predict because of a fluctuating labor participation rate, but said he expected a 9.5 percent unemployment rate by the end of 1997.
McCallum added that there was a high risk of a stock market correction in the long term, but he said he did not feel that would have an impact on Canada's economic fundamentals.
Per capita disposable income should rise in 1997 and 1998, partly through a hike in wages, but mainly due to a rise in the number of jobs, McCallum said.
